steps.title: Start with a square
steps.text: A square has two independent directions: across and up. Imagine dragging a copy in a new direction, joining each corner to its copy.
steps.hint: Drag to look around. The square is flat, even when you view it from the side.

steps.title: A square becomes a cube
steps.text: That new direction gives us a cube. Its boundary has six square faces; the two copies of our square are opposite faces.
steps.hint: Drag to orbit the cube. Scroll to zoom.

steps.title: A cube becomes a tesseract
steps.text: Drag a cube in a fourth independent direction and you get a tesseract. Its boundary has eight cube-shaped cells. We can only show a projection of it on this screen.
steps.hint: Count 16 corners and 32 edges in the strip below the model.

steps.title: A cube inside a cube?
steps.text: This is a perspective projection of a tesseract, looking along the fourth direction. The smaller cube is the farther cube-shaped cell; it is the same size as the nearer one in 4D.
steps.hint: Compare the two cubes, then go Next to change only the projection.

steps.title: A parallel shadow
steps.text: Orthographic projection uses parallel rays, so distance along the fourth direction does not shrink things. With this straight-on view, opposite cubes overlap. The tesseract still has all eight cells.
steps.hint: Shift-drag a little to separate the overlapping corners.

steps.title: A curved shadow
steps.text: For stereographic projection, we first map the boundary radially onto a 3-sphere in 4D. Projecting from one point on that sphere makes many edges curve. Geometry near the projection pole is clipped from this finite view.
steps.hint: Shift-drag slowly. This is a different map, not a change to the tesseract itself.

steps.title: Turn toward a new direction
steps.text: Watch a rotation in the XW plane: one familiar direction turns into the fourth direction. Cells seem to pass through each other or turn inside out in the shadow. The 4D shape stays rigid.
steps.hint: Ordinary drag moves the 3D camera. Shift-drag turns the shape in 4D.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.text: The automatic turn is paused. Hold Shift and drag on the model to turn it in 4D yourself. Overlaps in the projection do not mean the cells intersect in 4D.
steps.hint: Try the XW, YW and ZW turn pads too. Reset this step whenever you want.

title: A shape passing through our space

steps.title: Slice a tesseract
steps.text: The right view is a 3D slice through the tesseract, not its shadow. We sweep an angled cutting space from one side to the other. A 4D shape passing through our space would appear, change shape, and disappear like this.
steps.hint: After the sweep, move the Depth slider to explore at your own pace.

steps.title: Slice the 24-cell
steps.text: The 24-cell has 24 octahedral cells. Different depths reveal different 3D sections. The left view shows the whole shape; the right view shows only its intersection with our cutting space.
steps.hint: Replay the sweep, or drag Depth and watch the corners change.

steps.title: Eight cubes make a net
steps.text: A cube unfolds into six squares. A tesseract unfolds into eight cubes joined at square faces. This 3D cross is often called the Dalí cross; it could fold into a tesseract using the fourth direction.
steps.hint: Drag in the right view to orbit the real 3D cell arrangement.

steps.title: A net is not a shadow
steps.text: In the net, the cubes have moved apart by hinging around shared square faces. In the left-hand shadow, the cells are still in their original 4D positions. Both views refer to the same eight source cells.
steps.hint: Look for the central cube, its six neighbors, and the final cube at the end of one arm.

steps.title: The 5-cell
steps.text: There are six convex regular 4D polytopes, including the tesseract. The simplest is the 5-cell: five tetrahedral cells with five vertices. Its dual has the same shape type.
steps.hint: A dual swaps vertices with cells, and edges with faces.

steps.title: The 16-cell
steps.text: The 16-cell has 16 tetrahedral cells and eight vertices. It is the tesseract’s dual: the eight cube centers of a tesseract become its eight vertices, after suitable scaling.
steps.hint: Compare its eight vertices with the tesseract’s eight cells.

steps.title: The 24-cell
steps.text: The 24-cell has 24 octahedral cells and 24 vertices. It is self-dual, and has no regular counterpart in 3D.
steps.hint: Shift-drag to see the symmetry from another direction.

steps.title: The 120-cell and 600-cell
steps.text: The 120-cell has 120 dodecahedral cells and 600 vertices. Its dual, the 600-cell, has 600 tetrahedral cells and 120 vertices. Use the button to switch between this final dual pair.
steps.hint: These detailed shapes use an edge-only view so turning stays responsive. Finish returns to your previous document.
